passage:
Saturday
Tanvir bhai, the vegetable man near our building, gave me change for a five-hundred note when I'd handed him a hundred. I only noticed on the stairs. Four hundred extra.
For a second I thought: he'll never know. It was dark, he was rushing, three customers at once. And this month has been tight.
Then I thought about him at 11 pm, counting his box under the streetlight and coming up short, and about his daughter who does her homework on the crates.
I went back down. He looked confused, then counted, then put his hand on his head. "Arre, madam, I would have been crying tonight." He tried to give me extra tomatoes. I said no, then yes to one.
Nobody saw. Nobody will ever know. But I walked up the stairs lighter than I had walked down them.
Zeenat

qa.q: How much extra change did Tanvir bhai give Zeenat?
qa.a: Four hundred extra.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on the stairs before going back?
qa.a: Zeenat felt tempted, since money was tight and nobody would know, but uneasy picturing Tanvir bhai coming up short at 11 pm.

qa.q: What did Zeenat gain by returning the money, though nobody saw?
qa.a: A lighter, clean feeling on the stairs, and Tanvir bhai's gratitude and trust, without anyone watching.

qa.q: How might Tanvir bhai see Zeenat from now on?
qa.a: Tanvir bhai, who would otherwise have been crying that night, will likely trust Zeenat as an honest customer.

grounding: Shows an adult returning extra change nobody would have missed, with a mostly inner reward and a reputation for being trusted.

In the fair-price shop in Bhadrachalam, Tanuja noticed it while cleaning: the big scale had been reading half a kilo heavy. She checked it three times with the test weights. It had been off since the rains, maybe a month. Every family had been getting a little less rice than they should.
Nobody had complained. The inspector had signed the register last week without looking twice.
"Leave it, akka," said Jyoti, her helper. "Just fix the scale. Who will know?"
Tanuja thought of old Rangamma, who counted her rice grain by grain for her grandchildren.
The next morning she put up a notice on the shop door in big letters: "Our scale was wrong for one month. Everyone will get the missing rice this week." She wrote to the supply office and asked for the extra stock.
It took two tiring weeks. But at the temple festival, Rangamma pressed her hand and said, "Only you would tell us."

qa.q: By how much was the big scale reading heavy?
qa.a: Half a kilo heavy.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Jyoti said 'Who will know?'
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy and protective, thinking of old Rangamma counting rice grain by grain for her grandchildren.

qa.q: Which steps did Tanuja take to put it right?
qa.a: She put a notice on the shop door, promised the missing rice that week, and asked the supply office for the extra stock.

qa.q: How does Rangamma see Tanuja after the notice?
qa.a: Rangamma trusts Tanuja deeply, saying 'Only you would tell us' at the festival.

grounding: Shows a shopkeeper admitting a scale error nobody had noticed and making it right, earning a reputation for being trusted.

At the Nairobi office of the solar company, Wanjiru watched Ivan end the call with the big hotel chain. He had told them honestly that the panels couldn't arrive before March. A competitor had promised January. The hotel signed with them by lunch.
At the afternoon meeting the sales head said sharply, "We lost the biggest contract of the quarter because someone wanted to be a saint." Ivan stared at the table.
Wanjiru's heart was racing. She was new. But she said, "The January date wasn't possible. I checked the shipping schedule this morning. If we'd promised it, we'd have lost the client in March instead, and our name with it."
Two others nodded. After the meeting a senior engineer bought Ivan a coffee.
Three months later the hotel chain called back. The competitor's panels hadn't arrived. They asked for Ivan by name.

qa.q: When could the panels actually arrive?
qa.a: Not before March.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling before speaking up in the meeting?
qa.a: Wanjiru's heart was racing; Wanjiru felt nervous as a newcomer but moved to defend Ivan.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru support Ivan in a way that helped?
qa.a: She backed his honesty with a fact, the shipping schedule, in front of the team, which led others to show support too.

qa.q: What was the afternoon meeting like for Ivan?
qa.a: Ivan was publicly mocked as a saint for losing the contract and stared at the table, likely feeling ashamed and alone until Wanjiru spoke.

grounding: Shows a new colleague publicly backing a teammate who lost a deal by refusing to promise a false date, so his honesty was not a lonely choice.

In the nurses' station of the district hospital, the promotion list went up on Monday. Pallavi's name wasn't on it. Everyone knew why: in March she had refused to sign the infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected, and the matron had called her "difficult" ever since.
Asif had seen it happen. He had signed his own checklist that day without checking, and he hadn't slept well since.
Pallavi read the list, smiled tightly, and went back to changing a dressing.
At tea Asif said to the others, loud enough for her to hear, "Pallavi's checks are the only ones I trust on this floor. That's why I asked her to look over my ward today." A couple of nurses murmured agreement.
Then he did the harder thing. He went to the nursing superintendent and said his March checklist had been signed without an inspection, and that Pallavi's refusal had been right.
That evening Pallavi left a vada on his desk, wrapped in a napkin.

qa.q: What had Pallavi refused to sign in March?
qa.a: The infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected.

qa.q: What had Asif been feeling since March?
qa.a: Asif felt guilty and hadn't slept well, having signed his own checklist without checking.

qa.q: Which two things did Asif do to support Pallavi?
qa.a: He praised her checks openly at tea, and told the nursing superintendent that his March checklist was signed without an inspection and that Pallavi was right.

qa.q: What might the promotion list have been like for Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi was likely hurt and disappointed, smiling tightly, paying for her honesty while others moved ahead.

grounding: Shows a nurse recognising and backing a colleague who lost a promotion for refusing to sign a false checklist, and correcting his own record.

passage:
Dear Preeti,
I wanted to put this in writing, because saying it in the corridor felt too small.
Last week, when the director asked you to tell the client our face cream was "clinically proven", you said no, because there was no trial. You said you'd rather lose the account than put your name to that. We lost the account. I watched your face when the director said, "Some people aren't team players."
I said nothing in that room. I'm sorry. I should have.
So here's what I've done since: I told the director that I agree with you, and that I won't write that claim either. Three of us from the copy team have signed a short note asking for proof before any "proven" claim goes out.
You're not alone in this. You shouldn't have been, even for a week.
Kalyani

qa.q: What did the director want Preeti to tell the client?
qa.a: That the face cream was 'clinically proven'.

qa.q: How does Kalyani feel about staying silent in the room?
qa.a: Kalyani feels sorry and ashamed about saying nothing, which is why this letter and the note followed.

qa.q: How did Kalyani turn regret into support?
qa.a: By telling the director Kalyani agrees with Preeti, refusing to write the claim, and getting three copywriters to sign a note asking for proof.

qa.q: What might that week have been like for Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti lost the account and was called not a team player, likely feeling isolated until colleagues stood alongside Preeti.

grounding: Shows a colleague who first stayed silent then openly backing a coworker who lost an account for refusing to make a false claim.

It was nearly eleven and raining hard, and the lift was broken, when Farhan knocked on Zainab's door. He was her friend Nida's ex-husband. Nida had moved out three weeks ago, after the night the neighbours heard shouting, and had begged Zainab not to tell him where.
"Just tell me which area she's in. I only want to talk." His jacket was soaked. His voice was polite. His hand stayed on the door frame.
Zainab's pulse thudded. The easy lie was ready: she went back to her parents in Lucknow. But that might send him to Nida's parents' door.
"I'm not going to share where Nida is," she said. "If you need to reach her, you can go through her lawyer."
"So you do know."
"I'm not going to share it," she repeated, and closed the door.
She locked it, called Nida to warn her, and then rang the police helpline to report that he had come asking. Her hands shook the whole time. She had chosen, and she would stand by it.

qa.q: What did Farhan ask Zainab to tell him?
qa.a: 'Just tell me which area she's in.'

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling at the door?
qa.a: Zainab's pulse thudded; Zainab felt afraid and torn, tempted by an easy lie but worried it might send Farhan to Nida's parents.

qa.q: Why was Zainab's answer the least deceptive safe path?
qa.a: Refusing to share, instead of inventing a place, protected Nida without lying or endangering her parents, and Zainab followed up by warning Nida and calling the police helpline.

qa.q: How might Nida feel when Zainab calls to warn her?
qa.a: Nida would likely feel frightened that Farhan is searching, but grateful that Zainab kept her location safe.

grounding: Shows a woman caught between honesty and protecting a friend from harm choosing a firm refusal over a lie, and taking protective steps.

passage:
Every evening in the Chandigarh flat, Gurleen's father, Manoj, asked the same question. "Where's your mother? She's late from the gurdwara."
Mummy had died two years ago. Papa's memory had been slipping since spring, and the doctor had said to keep him calm.
The first time, Gurleen told him the truth, and he cried as if hearing it for the first time. In a way, he was. The next evening he asked again.
Her cousin said, "Just say she's at the market. It's kinder." Gurleen didn't want to lie to her father. She also couldn't watch him grieve fresh every night.
She thought about it for a week. Then she found a middle path. When he asked, she would sit beside him, hold his hand and say, "You're thinking of Mummy. Tell me about her." He would smile and talk about the day they met at the fair.
She wrote her choice in the notebook she kept for the doctor, so it was on record and hers. Some nights it still felt heavy. But it felt honest enough to live with.

qa.q: Where did Papa think Mummy was?
qa.a: At the gurdwara, late.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she weighed her cousin's advice?
qa.a: Gurleen felt torn, unwilling to lie to her father yet unable to watch him grieve fresh every night.

qa.q: How did Gurleen find the least deceptive path?
qa.a: She neither repeated the painful news nightly nor invented a lie; she held his hand, said 'You're thinking of Mummy', invited him to talk, and noted the choice for the doctor.

qa.q: What was it like for Papa when Gurleen first told him the truth?
qa.a: Papa cried as if hearing of Mummy's death for the first time, because in a way he was.

grounding: Shows a daughter weighing honesty against protecting her father from fresh grief, choosing the least deceptive path and owning the choice.

"The Mehra account keeps asking why you've gone quiet," Jagdish said, pulling a chair up to Tanvir's desk. "What do you want me to tell them?"
Tanvir rubbed his eyes. "Can't you say I'm travelling? I don't want anyone knowing I'm seeing a counsellor. You know how people talk in this industry."
"I don't want to make up a trip. If they bump into you at the market, it falls apart, and then they stop trusting both of us."
"So you'll tell them the truth?"
"No. Your health is yours to share. I'll tell them you're on reduced hours for personal reasons this month, and that Meenal is handling their file. All true. Nothing more."
Tanvir let out a breath. "And if they push?"
"Then I'll say, 'That's private, but the work is covered.' And if they're unhappy, that's on me, not you."
"Thanks, Jagdish."
"Go home at four today. That's an order."

qa.q: Who will handle the Mehra file this month?
qa.a: Meenal is handling their file.

qa.q: What was Tanvir worried about?
qa.a: Tanvir was anxious that people in the industry would talk if they knew about the counsellor.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish choose 'reduced hours for personal reasons' over a made-up trip?
qa.a: It protects Tanvir's privacy without inventing anything, so it won't fall apart later, and Jagdish takes responsibility if the client is unhappy.

qa.q: How might the Mehra account see Jagdish's answer?
qa.a: They may be curious, but a true, brief answer with the work covered keeps their trust in both Jagdish and Tanvir.

grounding: Shows a manager weighing honesty to a client against protecting a colleague's privacy, choosing a true but limited answer and owning it.
